questions.stem: Which change best illustrates the evolving concept of family in Australian law?
options: Married couples have been required to live together in the same home since federation
Parents have had no legal duties to their children since the Family Law Act 1975 began
Divorce has been restricted to cases where one spouse proves the other was at fault
Same-sex couples have been able to marry since the Marriage Act was amended in 2017
questions.explanation: The Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 redefined marriage as the union of two people, reflecting changed community values. Since 1975 divorce in Australia has been no-fault, and parents have always had legal duties to their children.

questions.stem: Which statement about the right to family under international law is correct?
options: The ICCPR recognises the family as the natural and fundamental group unit of society, entitled to protection
The UN Charter requires every state to register all families in a single international database
International law allows a state to forbid marriage between any two adults whose union the state disapproves of
The UDHR states that only married couples with children are entitled to be treated as a family
questions.explanation: Article 23 of the ICCPR, echoing Article 16 of the UDHR, says the family is entitled to protection by society and the state, and protects the right to marry and found a family. The UDHR also requires that marriage be entered into only with the free and full consent of the intending spouses.

questions.stem: Which is a main reason the law regulates family relationships?
options: To protect vulnerable family members, such as children, and resolve disputes when relationships break down
To allow the government to decide how many children each family is permitted to have in Australia
To make sure that every family follows the same religious beliefs and the same cultural traditions
To prevent adults from ending a marriage unless a court is satisfied the marriage was never valid
questions.explanation: Family law sets out rights and duties, protects children and people at risk of violence, and provides fair processes for separation, parenting and property. Australians can end a valid marriage by no-fault divorce.

questions.stem: Relationships Australia provides family dispute resolution services. What does this best show about the role of NGOs in family law?
options: NGOs decide whether a marriage is valid before it can be legally registered
NGOs replace the role of police in responding to incidents of family violence
NGOs help families resolve disputes outside court, reducing cost and conflict
NGOs make binding parenting orders that the Family Court must then enforce
questions.explanation: Community organisations deliver mediation, counselling and support that make the system more accessible. They cannot make binding orders, which only courts can do.

questions.stem: Under the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth), marriage is defined as:
options: the union of 2 people that has been registered with the NSW Relationships Register
the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life
the union of a man and a woman, entered into with the written consent of both of their parents
any relationship between 2 adults who have lived together continuously for 2 years
questions.explanation: This definition has applied since December 2017. A couple who live together without marrying may be in a de facto relationship, and the NSW Relationships Register records relationships, not marriages.

questions.stem: Which situation would make a marriage void under the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth)?
options: One party did not tell the other about a large debt owed to a credit card company
The couple married in a garden instead of in a registered place of worship
One party was already married to someone else at the time of the marriage
The couple had known each other for less than three months before marrying
questions.explanation: A marriage is void if a party is already married, the parties are in a prohibited relationship, a party did not really consent, or a party is not of marriageable age. A short courtship, undisclosed debts or the venue do not make a marriage void.

questions.stem: Ella and Tom, both 25, want to marry. Under the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth), what must they do before the wedding?
options: Give a notice of intended marriage to their celebrant at least one month beforehand
Obtain a certificate from a court confirming that both of them are of sound mind
Live together for at least two years so that they are recognised as a de facto couple
Obtain the written consent of both sets of parents, which is needed at every age
questions.explanation: A notice of intended marriage must generally be given at least one month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. Parental consent is needed only for a person under 18 who has a court order to marry, which is rare.

questions.stem: Under the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth), the marriageable age is 18. In what circumstances can a 17-year-old marry?
options: A 17-year-old may marry another 17-year-old once they have completed a pre-marriage education course
A 17-year-old can never marry in Australia, because the Act was amended to remove every exception
A judge or magistrate may authorise it in exceptional and unusual circumstances, and only to a person aged 18 or over
A 17-year-old may marry anyone if both of their parents give consent, without any need for a court order
questions.explanation: Section 12 lets a person aged 16 or 17 apply for a court order in exceptional and unusual circumstances, and they may marry only a person who is of marriageable age. Parental consent is also required, but it is not enough on its own.

questions.stem: Under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), which is a requirement before a court can make a property order for a de facto couple who have separated?
options: The couple must have held all their property in joint names during the whole relationship
Generally, the relationship lasted at least 2 years, or there is a child of the relationship
The couple must have registered their relationship with a court at the time they started living together
The couple must have been engaged to be married at the time the relationship came to an end
questions.explanation: A court can generally make orders if the de facto relationship lasted at least two years in total, there is a child, the relationship was registered, or a party made substantial contributions. Most states, including NSW, referred power over de facto financial matters to the Commonwealth, with effect from 2009.

questions.stem: In NSW, couples can have their relationship officially recorded under the Relationships Register Act 2010 (NSW). What is a main benefit of registering?
options: It allows the couple to avoid any property claims if the relationship later ends
It allows the couple to adopt a child without any assessment by the department
It provides clear proof that the relationship exists, without needing to prove its length
It turns the relationship into a legal marriage under the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth)
questions.explanation: Registration is evidence of the relationship for legal purposes such as property claims and entitlements. It is not a marriage, and it does not prevent property claims or replace adoption assessments.

questions.stem: Which is a main challenge in identifying and responding to forced marriages in Australia?
options: Police have no power to investigate forced marriage, because it is treated only as a civil matter
Forced marriage can only be reported by a person who has turned 21 years of age
Victims may be reluctant to report because doing so may involve reporting their own family
Forced marriage is lawful in Australia if the ceremony is performed outside a church
questions.explanation: Causing a person to enter a forced marriage has been a Commonwealth criminal offence since 2013, investigated by the Australian Federal Police. Many victims are young and fear family consequences, so cases are hidden and under-reported.

questions.stem: Under section 60CA of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), when making a parenting order the court must regard as the paramount consideration:
options: the child's own stated wishes
the parents' financial positions
the best interests of the child
the wishes of the parents
questions.explanation: The child's best interests are paramount in parenting decisions. The child's views are one factor the court considers, along with safety and the child's needs, but they do not decide the case.

questions.stem: Changes to the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) that began in May 2024 affected parenting cases mainly by:
options: removing the requirement to consider the safety of children when the court makes a parenting order
removing the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility and simplifying the best interests factors
creating a presumption that children spend equal time with each parent whatever their circumstances
requiring every parenting dispute to be decided by a civil jury of four in the Federal Circuit and Family Court
questions.explanation: The Family Law Amendment Act 2023 removed the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility and the link to equal time, and replaced the old list with a shorter set of best interests factors that begins with safety. Safety became more central, not less.

questions.stem: Under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), parental responsibility means:
options: the amount of time a child spends living with each parent after the parents' separation or divorce
the amount of child support that a parent pays to the other after their separation
the right of a parent to decide all matters without the other parent's knowledge
all the duties, powers and authority that by law parents have in relation to their children
questions.explanation: Parental responsibility covers decision-making and duties for a child under 18, and each parent has it unless a court orders otherwise. Time with a child and child support are separate matters.

questions.stem: Under the Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 (NSW), a teacher who suspects a student is at risk of significant harm must:
options: report it, because teachers are mandatory reporters
keep it confidential unless the parent gives consent
investigate personally before telling anyone else
report it only if the student asks them to do so
questions.explanation: Mandatory reporters, including teachers, health workers and police, must report reasonable grounds to suspect a child is at risk of significant harm. The department then assesses and investigates; teachers do not investigate themselves.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Child Placement Principles in NSW care law?
options: To require all children in out-of-home care to be placed with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander foster carers
To give the child's family the final power to decide every placement without involving the court
To keep Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in care connected to family, community and culture
To prevent Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from ever being placed in out-of-home care
questions.explanation: The principles set an order of preference for placement, starting with extended family or kin, and require participation of the child's family and community. Courts and the department still make placement decisions based on the child's safety.

questions.stem: Which statement about adoption in NSW is correct?
options: An adoption order lasts only until the child turns 16, when the birth parents' rights return
An adoption can be arranged privately between families without any court order
An adoption order allows the birth parents to keep sharing parental responsibility
An adoption order permanently transfers parental responsibility to the adoptive parents
questions.explanation: Under the Adoption Act 2000 (NSW), the Supreme Court makes adoption orders, which permanently transfer parental responsibility and must be in the child's best interests. Open adoption, with contact and information sharing, is encouraged, but birth parents no longer have parental responsibility.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a challenge in safeguarding children from abuse and neglect?
options: Abuse often happens in private and is under-reported, while removing children can itself cause harm
Child protection laws in NSW apply only to children under five, so most older children are unprotected
Mandatory reporting has been abolished in NSW, so the department relies only on police reports
Courts cannot make any orders about a child unless both parents agree to the orders proposed
questions.explanation: Harm to children is often hidden, and the system must balance protecting children with the trauma of removal and the right to family. NSW keeps mandatory reporting, and the Children's Court can make orders without parental agreement.

questions.stem: Under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), the only ground for divorce is:
options: a mutual agreement signed before the marriage began
a period of separation of at least 5 years
irretrievable breakdown, shown by 12 months of separation
proof that one spouse committed adultery or cruelty
questions.explanation: Australia has had no-fault divorce since 1975: the court must be satisfied the marriage has broken down irretrievably, shown by at least 12 months of separation with no reasonable likelihood of reconciliation. Fault is irrelevant to whether a divorce is granted.

questions.stem: Kim and Lee have been married for 18 months and have separated. What extra requirement applies if they apply for divorce?
options: Because they have been married for under 2 years, they must obtain the consent of their parents
Because they have been married for under 2 years, they generally need a counselling certificate
Because they have been married for under 2 years, they must first prove fault by one spouse
Because they have been married for under 2 years, they must have lived apart for 5 years
questions.explanation: For marriages of less than two years, the parties generally must have attended counselling about reconciliation, or obtain the court's permission to proceed. Fault is not required for any divorce.

questions.stem: Separated parents want parenting orders from the court. Under section 60I of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), what must they usually do first?
options: Receive written approval from the child's school about the arrangements
Make a genuine effort at family dispute resolution and obtain a certificate
Appear before a jury that will decide which parent should have the children
Obtain a divorce order, which must be made before any parenting order
questions.explanation: Parents must generally attempt family dispute resolution and get a section 60I certificate before applying, unless an exception such as family violence or urgency applies. Parenting orders can be made whether or not the parents are married or divorced.

questions.stem: Which statement about a parenting plan is correct?
options: It is a court order that the police must enforce if either parent later fails to follow it
It must be approved by the Children's Court before the parents can follow it
It can only be made after the parents have been divorced for at least 12 months
It is a written, signed and dated agreement between parents that is not legally enforceable
questions.explanation: Parenting plans are flexible and avoid court, but they cannot be enforced. Parents who want enforceable arrangements can ask the court for consent orders.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates family dispute resolution as a way of resolving parenting disputes?
options: It is decided by a judge in a closed court, so parents have no say in the arrangements made for their children
It is cheaper and less adversarial than court, but it may be unsuitable where there is family violence or a power imbalance
It produces binding orders that can be enforced by police, but it is more costly than litigation in most cases
It must be used in every case including those involving family violence, so it fully protects vulnerable parties
questions.explanation: FDR encourages parents to cooperate and reach their own agreements, but a party affected by violence may be unable to negotiate freely, which is why exceptions exist. Agreements reached in FDR are not binding unless made into consent orders.

questions.stem: Which agency administers child support assessments in Australia?
options: The NSW Police Force
Services Australia
The Family Court
NSW Fair Trading
questions.explanation: Services Australia assesses and can collect child support under the Child Support (Assessment) Act 1989 (Cth), using a formula based on income, care arrangements and the costs of children. Courts have only a limited role in child support.

questions.stem: When dividing property after separation, a court will consider each party's contributions. Which is counted as a contribution?
options: Only money earned by each party in paid employment outside the home
Only property that was bought in the name of a single party
Only gifts received from relatives before the relationship began
Unpaid work as a homemaker and parent, as well as income earned
questions.explanation: The Family Law Act recognises financial and non-financial contributions, including homemaking and parenting. The court also considers each party's current and future circumstances, and since June 2025 it must consider the economic effects of family violence.

questions.stem: In Stanford v Stanford (2012), the High Court emphasised that before making a property order a court must be satisfied that:
options: it is just and equitable to make an order at all
the parties have been divorced for at least 2 years
each party will receive exactly half of the property
both parties have agreed to the order in writing
questions.explanation: The High Court held that the court must first be satisfied it is just and equitable to make any order altering property interests, rather than assuming an order will follow. There is no presumption of equal division.

questions.stem: Which statement about binding financial agreements under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) is correct?
options: They may only be made after a divorce order has been granted by the Federal Circuit and Family Court
They can never be set aside by a court once both parties have signed them in front of a witness
They decide parenting arrangements for children, so the best interests principle does not apply
Each party must receive independent legal advice before signing for the agreement to be binding
questions.explanation: Binding financial agreements can be made before, during or after a relationship, and each party must have independent legal advice. In Thorne v Kennedy (2017) the High Court set aside agreements made under undue influence.

questions.stem: Under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), what is the time limit for a former spouse to apply for property orders after a divorce order takes effect?
options: 3 years
6 years
12 months
18 months
questions.explanation: A former spouse has 12 months after the divorce takes effect, while separated de facto partners have 2 years from separation. After those limits, the court's permission is needed.

questions.stem: In NSW, a court order that protects a person from violence, harassment or intimidation by a family member or partner is called:
options: an apprehended domestic violence order
an apprehended personal violence order
a community correction order
a parenting order
questions.explanation: ADVOs are made under the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) where there is a domestic relationship. An APVO covers people who are not in a domestic relationship, such as neighbours.

questions.stem: Which statement about ADVOs in NSW is correct?
options: Police can apply for an ADVO, and breaching an ADVO is a criminal offence
An ADVO is a criminal conviction recorded against the person it restrains
Only the person in need of protection may apply, and police cannot assist
An ADVO can only be made after the defendant has been convicted of assault
questions.explanation: Police must apply in many cases and can issue provisional orders, and the court may make an order without any conviction. An ADVO is a civil order, but breaching it is a criminal offence.

questions.stem: Since 1 July 2024, coercive control has been a criminal offence in NSW. The offence targets:
options: conduct by parents who set reasonable household rules, such as curfews, for their teenage children
a single act of physical violence by a stranger against a victim in a public street or at a shopping centre
a course of abusive conduct against a current or former intimate partner intended to coerce or control them
any single argument between family members in which one person shouts at the other in their own home
questions.explanation: Section 54D of the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) makes it an offence to engage in a course of abusive behaviour towards an intimate partner, intending to coerce or control them. It recognises that much family violence is a pattern of non-physical abuse, which earlier laws struggled to capture.

questions.stem: Which is an example of support available to victims of domestic and family violence in NSW?
options: Automatic sole ownership of the family home once a complaint is made to police
Help from a Women's Domestic Violence Court Advocacy Service to obtain an ADVO
The right to choose the sentence imposed on the offender at a criminal trial
A guaranteed payment from the offender before any criminal case can begin
questions.explanation: Court advocacy services support victims through ADVO proceedings, and other services provide crisis accommodation, counselling and legal help. Victims do not set sentences or receive automatic property transfers.

questions.stem: When the Department of Communities and Justice believes a child is in need of care and protection, which court may make care orders?
options: The Land and Environment Court
The Children's Court of NSW
The NSW Court of Appeal
The High Court of Australia
questions.explanation: The Children's Court hears care and protection applications and can make orders such as allocating parental responsibility to the Minister. In these proceedings the safety, welfare and wellbeing of the child are paramount.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant barrier to protecting vulnerable people from family violence?
options: Family violence is not recognised as a crime in NSW, so police cannot charge any perpetrator
ADVOs can only be made by the High Court, which few victims can afford to approach
Victims are required to pay a fee to police before any report of violence is investigated
Many victims do not report because of fear, financial dependence or a wish to keep the family together
questions.explanation: Under-reporting is driven by fear of retaliation, economic dependence, isolation, cultural or language barriers and distrust of authorities. Family violence offences can be charged, and ADVOs are made in the Local Court.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the effectiveness of ADVOs?
options: They are ineffective because breaching one carries no penalty of any kind under NSW law
They can be obtained quickly and cheaply, but they rely on reporting and enforcement and are often breached
They guarantee that a victim will never again be harmed, so no further support services are needed
They are rarely used because they require a full criminal trial before a jury in the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: ADVOs are a key protective tool and are made in large numbers, but a piece of paper cannot stop a determined offender, and breaches are common. Effectiveness depends on police responses, support services and the courts.

questions.stem: Which UN convention requires the best interests of the child to be a primary consideration in all actions concerning children?
options: The Genocide Convention
The Convention on the Rights of the Child
The Convention against Torture
The Refugee Convention
questions.explanation: Article 3 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which Australia ratified in 1990, sets out the best interests principle. It is reflected in the Family Law Act 1975 and NSW care and protection law.
